item.title: Breeding examinations
item.description:
Recognised eye examinations for breeding animals help to detect hereditary eye diseases early – before they lead to clinical signs. This benefits the individual animal as well as responsible breeding decisions.

Procedure

We examine individual breeding animals or entire litters according to the recognised DOK/ECVO guidelines, including examination of the drainage angle (gonioscopy) for breeds at risk. For breed clubs, group appointments with several animals are possible by arrangement, also outside our practice on request. We are also happy to advise you in general on hereditary eye diseases in your breed.

item.title: Corneal diseases and reconstructive corneal surgery
item.description:
The cornea is the clear, sensitive front surface of the eye. If it is injured, inflamed or becomes cloudy, this usually shows as a red, watering or squinted eye.

When you should see us

  • a suddenly painful, watering or squinted eye
  • visible cloudiness or a whitish, greyish or dark spot on the cornea
  • a corneal defect that does not heal despite treatment by your family vet
  • chronic, sticky eye discharge or recurring conjunctivitis

Common conditions

  • injuries and ulcers of the cornea, including deep or already perforated defects
  • persistent, non-healing defects such as SCCED (“boxer ulcer”)
  • chronic inflammation, for example the hereditary pannus disease in German Shepherds
  • infections, among others with feline herpesvirus
  • cornea nigra (corneal sequestrum) – a blackish tissue necrosis that occurs mainly in short-nosed cat breeds
  • dermoids – congenital, hairy islands of skin on the cornea that rub constantly
  • dry eye and foreign bodies

What we examine

We stain the corneal surface with a special dye (fluorescein) – defects show up green, even when they are barely visible to the naked eye.

item.title: Eyelid, eyelash and third eyelid surgery
item.description:
Changes to the eyelids, eyelashes or the third eyelid often rub directly on the sensitive cornea – the actual discomfort is then caused by this friction.

When you should see us

  • an eyelid rolled inwards or outwards (entropion/ectropion)
  • a visible swelling or lump on the eyelid margin
  • a red, bulging swelling in the inner corner of the eye (prolapsed third eyelid gland, commonly called “cherry eye”)
  • persistent watering, squinting or rubbing despite normal-looking eyelids – often a tiny, hidden eyelash is behind it
  • in short-nosed breeds such as Pugs or French Bulldogs: chronic eye discharge or dark discolouration of the cornea

What we examine

During the examination we carefully pull forward the third eyelid to check whether a foreign body, a hidden eyelash or a change to the third eyelid gland is hiding behind it.

item.title: Glaucoma and painful eyes
item.description:
Glaucoma is excessively high pressure inside the eye. Left untreated, it damages the optic nerve and retina within a few hours – an acute glaucoma attack is therefore an emergency in which every hour counts.

When you should see us

  • a suddenly red, cloudy or unusual-looking eye
  • pupils of different sizes
  • your pet squints one eye, is noticeably quiet or eating less
  • glaucoma has already been diagnosed in one eye and the second eye needs to be checked

What we examine

We measure the intraocular pressure (tonometry) and use the slit lamp and a special lens to look into the drainage angle (gonioscopy) – the narrow passage through which the fluid inside the eye normally drains. This lets us tell whether a congenital malformation, inflammation or another cause lies behind the raised pressure.

item.title: Inner eye, lens and cataract
item.description:
The inner eye includes the iris, the anterior chamber and the lens. The most common condition that owners notice themselves is cataract – a clouding of the lens that can lead to blindness.

When you should see us

  • a greyish or whitish cloudiness in the pupil
  • a sudden deterioration in vision, for example bumping into furniture or uncertainty in the dark
  • your pet has diabetes – diabetes can lead to cataract very quickly
  • a red, painful eye with a small pupil as a possible sign of inflammation inside the eye (uveitis)

What we examine

We assess the lens, iris and anterior chamber with the slit lamp and check for inflammation inside the eye or a displaced lens. Before any possible surgery, we also use ultrasound and a retinal function test (electroretinogram) to check whether the retina behind the clouded lens is still intact – this is decisive for whether surgery can really benefit vision.

item.title: Retinal diagnostics and investigation of vision problems
item.description:
Sudden or gradual loss of vision has many possible causes – from a primary retinal disease to a general illness such as high blood pressure that shows up in the eye first.

When you should see us

  • your pet suddenly bumps into objects or can no longer find its way in the dark
  • conspicuously wide pupils that don’t react to light – an alarm signal, especially in older cats
  • a gradual deterioration in vision noticed by you or your family vet
  • known kidney disease, thyroid disease or high blood pressure

What we examine

With ophthalmoscopy we examine the retina for detachment, bleeding, inflammation or degeneration.

item.title: Tear ducts and surgical treatment of dry eye
item.description:
A healthy tear film keeps the ocular surface moist and protected. If there is too little tear fluid or it has the wrong composition (dry eye), or if the tear drainage ducts are narrowed, the ocular surface suffers permanently.

When you should see us

  • sticky, greyish or yellowish mucus in the eye
  • a chronically watering eye without any visible injury
  • already visible clouding or pigmentation of the cornea, especially in short-nosed breeds

What we examine

With the Schirmer tear test we measure tear production to reliably diagnose dry eye. If a narrowed tear drainage is suspected, we check and flush the tear ducts.
